text: 7-year-old boy. The patient has been experiencing recurrent episodes lasting 3–4 minutes each of facial grimacing and staring over the past month. During these episodes, he is nonresponsive and does not recall them afterward. He reports a muddy taste in his mouth before the onset of these episodes. His brother witnessed him waking up, staring, and making hand gestures during one episode. The patient felt lethargic and confused afterwards.

speaker: Doctor
text: Does he experience any rhythmic jerking movements or stiffening of his limbs during these episodes? Have you noticed if these spells happen more frequently at night or upon waking?

speaker: Doctor
text: REQUEST TEST: EEG. Given the muddy taste aura, focal motor signs like hand gestures, and post-ictal confusion, I strongly suspect focal seizures originating from the temporal lobe.

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Electroencephalogram: Interictal spikes and sharp waves localized to the temporal lobes, more prominent on the right side.

speaker: Doctor
text: The EEG confirms focal epilepsy, likely right temporal lobe in origin. Do you have any history of head trauma, fever, or infections around the time these episodes began? Also, have you noticed any changes in his memory, behavior, or school performance recently?

speaker: Patient
text: Past medical history: No significant previous medical history. No prior seizures or neurological evaluations. Social history: Enrolled in second grade. Lives with parents and one sibling. No reported use of medications or exposure to toxins.

speaker: Doctor
text: Do you recall any specific illnesses like meningitis, encephalitis, or a high fever in the weeks or months leading up to these first episodes? Also, has his teacher reported any sudden changes in his memory, behavior, or academic performance at school?

speaker: Doctor
text: Given the focal onset and temporal lobe involvement, I need to rule out structural causes like a tumor or cortical dysplasia. REQUEST IMAGES: MRI Brain. Have there been any recent head injuries, even minor ones, that you might have overlooked?
